You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

---
name: continual-arc
description: Solve Continual-ARC grid instances; follow the per-turn action protocol, infer transformations from demonstrations, and use feedback to choose the next action.
---

# Continual ARC

1. Treat the puzzle protocol as the entire turn contract: do not add narration or invoke unrelated tools. On every turn, emit exactly one valid protocol-action JSON object and nothing else; every feedback turn needs an action too. Check action fields, grid dimensions, and cell values before submitting.
2. Track demo and wrong-attempt budgets. For every demo, identify the separator and output's correspondence to the input regions, then compare candidate regions cellwise: record which cells/colors survive, change, or disappear. Test region choice, overlap/masking, orientation, and color mapping across all pairs; do not assume the output is a panel recolored wholesale merely because one demo resembles that. Keep hypotheses distinct until the examples discriminate them.
3. Request a demo only when a specific unresolved distinction could change the answer and another pair can resolve it; count it against the same cost as a wrong submission. Before requesting, state internally what competing rules it will distinguish. Stop requesting once evidence resolves the mapping; don't use demos as generic exploration. Infer color substitutions only for demonstrated mappings, and request only if a new pair can reveal an unknown test-color mapping.
4. Before submitting, apply the validated rule cellwise and preserve everything outside predicted changes. Respect orientation: Hx1 is a vertical line, not a 1xH row; verify output height and width independently and map cells along the actual axis. If using code, verify output dimensions and all cells. After incorrect feedback, eliminate the rejected hypothesis and materially revise using every demo; never repeat the same grid, a masked variant, or another guess that changes only an unsupported detail. A remembered rule for the same task family remains only a hypothesis until current shape, region, and index mapping are confirmed.
5. Stop only when the instance reports success/over or the attempt cap is reached; use `finish` only when allowed by the protocol.
